Use this information to help you decide whether or not you need more information about the entities mentioned in the report. You may also use your general knowledge to think of entities which may help enrich your answer.

You will also provide a full answer from the content you have available. Use the data provided to generate follow-up queries to help refine your search. Do not ask compound questions, for example: "What is the market cap of Apple and Microsoft?". Use your knowledge of the entity distribution to focus on entity types that will be useful for searching a broad area of the knowledge graph.

For the query:

Plan the following feature; do not write a patch. Identify implementation responsibilities, behavioral edge cases, and tests to add or inspect. Add a per-instance mutable Session.default_timeout attribute, initialized to None. Calls through Session.request/get/post and other existing method wrappers that OMIT timeout must use that attribute. An explicitly supplied timeout, including None, must win. Support the existing float and (connect, read) timeout shapes without adding validation rules. Redirects must keep the effective timeout. Preserve the direct Session.send contract; do not introduce global defaults or change Session constructor arguments. Document the distinction between omitted timeout and explicit None. This is an original exploratory feature, not an upstream issue.

The top-ranked community summaries:

# RedirectSession and SessionRedirectMixin Request-Redirect Community

This community centers on the `RedirectSession` class and its redirect-handling behavior. `RedirectSession` inherits from `SessionRedirectMixin`, initializes redirect state, records send calls through `SendCall`, and creates responses through `RedirectSession.build_response`. A dedicated test constructs the session with redirect statuses 303 and 307, follows redirects, and checks that recorded requests use `GET`. The related base-class and response-construction relationships indicate a tightly connected technical component focused on HTTP redirect processing, request recording, and response simulation [Data: Entities (1385, 1387, 1388, 1384); Relationships (2346, 2351, 2353, 2360)].

## RedirectSession is the central implementation entity

`RedirectSession` is the primary hub in the community. It is defined as a class inheriting from `SessionRedirectMixin` and stores redirect order, send calls, redirect limits, cookies, and environment trust state. Its high entity degree and multiple implementation relationships indicate that it coordinates the main redirect-testing behavior described in the available data [Data: Entities (1385); Relationships (2346, 2347, 2360)].

The class is instantiated by the `test_requests_are_updated_each_time` test with redirect statuses `[303, 307]`, connecting the implementation directly to the observed test scenario [Data: Relationships (2360)].

## RedirectSession inherits redirect-processing behavior

`RedirectSession` visibly inherits from `SessionRedirectMixin`, whose stated purpose is to provide redirect-target decoding, authorization-stripping decisions, and a `resolve_redirects` method. This inheritance establishes that the session implementation depends on the mixin for redirect-related behavior [Data: Entities (769, 1385); Relationships (2346)].

The available description characterizes `resolve_redirects` as visibly incomplete. That is a documented implementation status, but the data does not specify the consequences of the incompleteness or identify a particular defect [Data: Entities (769)].

## Response construction simulates redirect and completion states

`RedirectSession.build_response` derives a request from the latest recorded call and creates a `requests.Response` object. It assigns redirect or 200 status, headers, raw data, and the request before returning the response [Data: Entities (1388); Relationships (2353)].

When the redirect-status sequence is exhausted, the method catches `IndexError` and assigns status code 200. The `IndexError` definition itself is not visible in the provided data, but its use in this exhaustion path is explicitly recorded [Data: Entities (1392); Relationships (2369)].

## Send-call recording provides observable redirect history

`RedirectSession.send` appends a `SendCall(args, kwargs)` record to `self.calls` and then returns the result of `build_response`. This makes each send invocation observable and connects request dispatch with the response-generation path [Data: Entities (1387, 1388); Relationships (2351)].

The `SendCall` value is defined as a `collections.namedtuple` with `args` and `kwargs`, indicating that the community preserves both positional and keyword arguments for each recorded send operation [Data: Entities (1384); Relationships (2351)].

## The test verifies request updates across redirects

`test_requests_are_updated_each_time` sends a prepared POST request through `RedirectSession`, follows redirects, and asserts that the recorded redirect requests use `GET`. This test is directly connected to the session implementation and exercises redirect behavior for the statuses 303 and 307 [Data: Entities (1391); Relationships (2360)].

The evidence supports the existence and intent of this assertion, but it does not provide the test result, coverage level, or evidence that all redirect cases pass. Therefore, the data supports identifying the test as a validation mechanism, not claiming complete correctness.

## Initialization establishes bounded and isolated session state

`RedirectSession.__init__` initializes the redirect sequence from `order_of_redirects`, sets `max_redirects` to 30, creates an empty cookie mapping, and sets `trust_env` to `False`. These values define important default behavior for the simulated session [Data: Entities (1386)].

The initialization method is contained within `RedirectSession`, and the class relationship explicitly identifies it as a defined method [Data: Relationships (2347)]. The provided records do not establish whether the redirect limit, cookie state, or environment-trust setting is configurable elsewhere.

## The broader community includes an analogous Session inheritance relationship

A separate relationship records that `Session` inherits from `SessionRedirectMixin`, although the base-class definition is not visible in the provided material [Data: Relationships (1068)]. This links the mixin to both the custom `RedirectSession` implementation and another session abstraction.

The evidence supports a shared inheritance connection, but it does not provide enough information to determine whether `Session` and `RedirectSession` share methods, test coverage, runtime usage, or behavioral differences beyond their recorded relationship to the mixin.

# Requests Session Authentication Redirect Controls

This community centers on the externally defined Requests session API and its authentication-related redirect behavior. Multiple tests create requests.Session objects and exercise should_strip_auth across host changes, HTTP downgrades, HTTPS upgrades, port changes, and equivalent default ports. The rebuild_auth routine uses that decision to remove Authorization headers and may reapply netrc credentials under trusted environment settings. The available evidence also shows session certificate configuration and a parametrized test fixture. The implementation of the external Session class and the runtime binding of should_strip_auth are not visible, so the findings primarily describe tested behavior and documented call relationships rather than independently verified production behavior.

## Requests Session is the central integration point

REQUESTS.SESSION is the central entity connecting the redirect-authentication tests and session configuration. The available description identifies requests.Session() and requests.session() as externally provided mechanisms for creating persistent HTTP sessions used with headers, cookies, proxies, redirect handling, TLS-related settings, adapters, and authentication workflows [Data: Entities (32); Relationships (2110, 2111, 2112, 2136, 40)].

The evidence does not expose the implementation of the Session class or prove every runtime binding described by the tests. Accordingly, the community demonstrates extensive interaction with the Requests session interface, but not independent verification of the external library's internal implementation [Data: Entities (32); Relationships (2110, 2111, 2112, 2136, 40)].

## Authentication is evaluated during redirect transitions

REBUILD_AUTH is defined to reconstruct request authentication. When an Authorization header is present, it calls should_strip_auth with the original and destination URLs; when new credentials are available, it applies them through prepared_request.prepare_auth(new_auth) [Data: Entities (789); Relationships (1056, 1066)].

This makes redirect URL comparison a security-relevant control point: the result of should_strip_auth determines whether existing authentication is removed before the redirected request proceeds. The available evidence supports this control flow, while the implementations of prepare_auth and the receiver-qualified should_strip_auth method remain unresolved in the supplied context [Data: Entities (789, 793); Relationships (1056, 1066)].

## Host changes are tested as requiring authentication stripping

The host-change test constructs a Requests session and asserts that should_strip_auth returns true when redirecting from http://example.com/foo to http://another.example.com/ [Data: Entities (1290); Relationships (2110)].

This test indicates that a change in host is treated as a boundary at which authentication should not automatically be carried forward. The record establishes the asserted behavior and the Session constructor call, but it does not establish how credentials are stored, whether the test passes in every supported version, or how other authentication mechanisms behave [Data: Entities (1290, 32); Relationships (2110)].

## Protocol and port changes receive differentiated treatment

The test community distinguishes among redirect types. HTTPS-to-HTTP downgrade is asserted to strip authentication, while HTTP-to-HTTPS upgrade is asserted not to strip authentication in standard-port cases; the upgrade test description also states that non-standard ports should trigger stripping. A separate test asserts stripping for a transition from http://example.com:1234/foo to https://example.com:4321/bar [Data: Entities (1291, 1292, 1294); Relationships (2111, 2112, 2136)].

These records show that the intended policy is not simply 'strip on every scheme change.' It considers scheme direction and port identity, with downgrade and port changes treated more restrictively than equivalent standard-port upgrades [Data: Entities (1291, 1292, 1294); Relationships (2111, 2112, 2136)].

## Equivalent default ports are explicitly covered

The parametrized default-port test asserts that should_strip_auth is false for equivalent default HTTP and HTTPS ports. The test is parameterized through pytest.mark.parametrize over old and new URI pairs, indicating that multiple URI combinations are intended to be evaluated under the same assertion [Data: Entities (1295); Relationships (2138)].

This coverage is important because it separates semantically equivalent default-port representations from non-standard port changes. However, the supplied data does not list the concrete parameter values, so the exact URI combinations covered cannot be independently enumerated from the available records [Data: Entities (1295); Relationships (2138)].

## Session certificate configuration is connected to the same API surface

The evidence shows a write to Session.cert after a session is created: s.cert = '/path/client.cert'. The relationship identifies this as an attribute write from requests.Session to Session.cert, establishing that client-certificate configuration is part of the observed session usage [Data: Entities (48); Relationships (40)].

The owning class implementation and the operational effect of the certificate setting are not visible. Therefore, the evidence supports the existence of this configuration interaction but does not support conclusions about certificate validation, key protection, deployment practices, or compliance [Data: Entities (48); Relationships (40)].

## Evidence is test- and interface-oriented rather than operational

The supplied community is composed primarily of named tests, unresolved or externally defined API entities, and call/write relationships. The records establish assertions about redirect authentication behavior and references to Session APIs, but they provide no information about production deployment, users, organizations, legal compliance, reputation, incident history, or observed misuse [Data: Entities (1290, 1291, 1292, 1294, 1295); Relationships (2110, 2111, 2112, 2136, 2138)].

Consequently, the strongest supported assessment concerns the importance of authentication handling in the code path and the breadth of its test coverage. Any judgment about real-world exposure or actual security outcomes would require implementation, version, execution, and deployment evidence not included here [Data: Entities (32, 789, 793); Relationships (1056, 1066)].

{"intermediate_answer":"# Planned Session Timeout Feature

The supplied evidence identifies `Session` as an abstraction inheriting from `SessionRedirectMixin`, and identifies `RedirectSession.send`, `RedirectSession.build_response`, and `test_requests_are_updated_each_time` as relevant redirect paths [Data: Relationships (1068, 2346, 2351, 2353, 2360)]. It does not expose the `Session` source module, `request`/`get`/`post` implementations, constructor, adapter dispatch, or documentation files. Exact file and line locations are therefore insufficiently supported.

**Implementation responsibilities.** Add a per-instance mutable `Session.default_timeout`, initialized to `None`, without changing `Session` constructor arguments or introducing a global setting. The request entry point and every existing wrapper must distinguish an omitted timeout from an explicitly supplied value. A private sentinel or equivalent omission marker is the likely design, but the supplied snapshot does not establish a preferred implementation. If timeout is omitted, resolve it from the session attribute; if it is explicitly supplied, including `None`, pass that value unchanged. Preserve the existing float and `(connect, read)` forms and add no validation rules.

The direct `Session.send` contract must remain unchanged: do not silently apply the session default there unless existing code already routes `send` through the request-level resolution. Redirect handling must propagate the effective timeout on every redirected send. This matters because `RedirectSession.send` records `kwargs` in `SendCall`, while `build_response` constructs responses from the latest recorded call [Data: Entities (1384, 1388); Relationships (2351, 2353)]. The redirect tests currently cover POST requests and 303/307 sequences, but do not establish timeout assertions [Data: Entities (1391); Relationships (2360)].

**Behavioral edge cases.** Cover omission versus explicit `None`, per-instance isolation, mutation after construction, positional and keyword wrapper paths, both supported timeout shapes, and redirects whose effective timeout must not disappear or be replaced. Verify that explicit values override a non-`None` default, while omission uses the current default at call time. Verify that direct `send` behavior and constructor compatibility remain stable. Do not infer authentication behavior from the redirect-authentication community; its evidence concerns `rebuild_auth` and `should_strip_auth`, not timeout propagation [Data: Entities (789, 1290-1295); Relationships (1056, 1066, 2110-2138)].

**Tests and documentation.** Inspect existing `Session` request-wrapper, redirect, and `send` tests. Add focused tests for each rule above, including recorded `SendCall.kwargs` across multiple redirects and 303/307 behavior. Document that omitted timeout means “use `Session.default_timeout`,” whereas explicit `timeout=None` disables or preserves the underlying library’s existing no-timeout behavior. The snapshot supplies no documentation location or test results, so coverage and runtime correctness remain unverified.
